opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a common picture where the key step is getting AI systems that can write code as well as a top engineer, and then you get this rapid feedback loop where AI improves AI. But when you look at what drives progress in AI, programming is only one part of it, and maybe not the bottleneck.

A lot of recent progress has come from scaling: more compute, more data, bigger training runs. Automating programming doesn't directly give you more chips or more electricity. If an AI system writes training code ten times faster, but the training run still takes months on a fixed number of GPUs, you haven't sped things up much. It's like Amdahl's law: if you dramatically accelerate one part of a process, the overall speedup is limited by the parts you didn't accelerate.

Then there's the research side, which is about knowing which experiments to run, having good taste about which directions are promising, interpreting surprising results, and deciding where to spend scarce compute. That's quite different from implementing a well-specified task. A lot of the most important advances, like new architectures, new training paradigms, and the shift toward reinforcement learning and inference-time compute, came from researchers having the right ideas at the right time, not from anyone typing code faster.

So for the feedback loop to really take off, you'd need AI systems that can automate research judgment as well, and probably help relax the physical constraints, through better chip design, more efficient algorithms that need less compute per unit of capability, or faster building of data centres and energy infrastructure. Otherwise you get a modest speedup, which matters, but you don't get the dramatic compression of timelines some people expect.

It's also possible that automating coding helps more than I'm suggesting, for example if there's a big overhang of good ideas that are only held back by engineering effort. But I'm not convinced that's the main constraint right now. I think people should be careful about assuming that because coding is what these systems are getting good at, coding must be the crux of AI progress.

r001.rationale: It contrasts implementing a well-specified task with research judgment about experiments and promising directions, and identifies new architectures as research advances.

r002.rationale: It says coding ten times faster or dramatically accelerating programming may yield limited overall speedup, but does not state that making programming instantaneous might do little.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: Well, I think the picture a lot of people have in their heads goes something like this: AI systems get good enough at writing code that they can do the work of the AI researchers at the frontier labs, and then you get this feedback loop where the AI improves itself, each generation builds the next one faster, and timelines collapse. And I understand why that picture is compelling. But when you actually look at what AI development consists of, programming turns out to be only one piece of it, and perhaps not the piece that's doing most of the work.

Think about what the bottlenecks really are. There's compute. There's data. There's the physical infrastructure, the data centres and the chips and the energy. And there's the research taste side of things: deciding which experiments are worth running, interpreting ambiguous results, having the judgement to say "this direction is a dead end, let's try something else." If you automate the programming and nothing else, you've sped up one input to a process that has several inputs, and the overall rate of progress is constrained by whichever input is slowest.

So suppose you make your researchers, in effect, ten times more productive at writing code. If running the experiments still takes the same amount of wall-clock time because you're waiting on GPUs, and if the training runs themselves still take months, then you've made the easy part faster and left the hard part untouched. The team is now sitting around waiting for results more than they used to, rather than iterating ten times as fast.

And I think there's a deeper point here about what research actually is. A lot of the most important advances in AI have not come from someone writing a cleverer implementation. They've come from conceptual insights: the transformer architecture, scaling laws, the idea that you could get a lot out of reinforcement learning from human feedback. Those are judgements about what to try. If AI systems could only write code to specification, they would be a very useful tool, but they wouldn't be the thing that generates the specification in the first place.

So when I hear people say "once AI can automate programming, we'll get an intelligence explosion," my reaction is that it would need to automate a much broader slice of the research process, including the experimental design, the scientific judgement, and probably some of the ways we get around the compute constraints, before you'd see timelines shorten dramatically. That's not impossible. But it's a higher bar than just being a very good coder, and I think it's worth being clear-eyed about that, because it affects how much time we think we have to get the safety side of things right.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts writing code to specification with discovering research directions, architectural insights, and which experiments to run.

r002.rationale: It says automating programming alone speeds up only one input, leaving progress constrained by slower inputs such as compute and experiment time, so timelines may shorten little.

astra-6.text:
Well, programming is only one part of AI research. There’s also coming up with promising ideas, designing experiments, running them, and working out what the results tell you. If you automate writing the code, you might make that part enormously faster, but then you’re waiting on the other parts.

For example, if an experiment requires a large training run, producing the code in a minute instead of a week doesn’t make the training run instantaneous. You may still be constrained by compute, or by your ability to decide which experiment is worth running next.

So the question is how much of the whole process these systems can accelerate. If they can also help generate better research ideas and find ways to test them more efficiently, then you could get a much larger speed-up. Automating programming could certainly help, but it doesn’t by itself establish that the time needed to develop the next generation of AI will become dramatically shorter.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes coding from broader research tasks such as generating ideas and designing experiments, but does not specify discovering which architectural changes will solve outstanding problems.

r002.rationale: It says that automating code writing alone does not establish dramatically shorter AI development timelines and gives slow training runs and experiment choices as remaining constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, programming is only one part of AI research. You also have to work out what experiments to run, understand what the results mean, and come up with new ideas about how to make these systems better. If you automate writing the code but those other parts still depend on humans, they could become the bottleneck.

There are also constraints that aren’t just about intellectual work. You might need a large training run to find out whether an idea works, and that takes time and compute. Producing the code much faster doesn’t necessarily make the experiment finish much faster.

So I’d distinguish between automating programming and automating the whole process of AI research. The former could certainly help. But to get a very substantial acceleration, you’d probably need systems that can take on more of that research process, or some reason to think that programming was overwhelmingly the limiting factor.

r001.rationale: It separates programming from broader research tasks such as choosing experiments and generating ideas, but does not specifically distinguish implementing a known goal from discovering which architectural changes solve outstanding problems.

r002.rationale: It says faster code writing may not substantially accelerate research because experiments take time and other work can be a bottleneck, but does not state that making programming instantaneous might do little to shorten AI development timelines.
